splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps agency deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous provisions in the Sentencing Guidelines or criminal statutes.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts should defer to agency interpretations that expand criminal liability when a guideline or statute is ambiguous, or whether the rule of lenity requires courts to adopt the less punitive reading. This matters because it determines whether agencies can effectively expand criminal sentences through interpretive guidance.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency deference in criminal contexts, requiring courts to adopt the less punitive interpretation of ambiguous provisions rather than deferring to agency readings that expand liability.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency deference to the Sentencing Commission's commentary takes precedence over the rule of lenity, allowing anti-defendant readings of ambiguous Guidelines provisions when supported by agency interpretation.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which expands the definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy, is a valid and binding interpretation of the guideline text after Kisor v. Wilkie.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Sentencing Commission's commentary adding inchoate offenses (conspiracy, attempt, aiding and abetting) to the career-offender guideline's definition of 'controlled substance offense' is entitled to deference when the guideline text itself does not mention such offenses. This affects thousands of federal sentences annually.

positions.label: Commentary is binding
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation entitled to deference under Stinson, and that inchoate offenses qualify as controlled substance offenses for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Commentary exceeds guideline text
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses and that Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the definition beyond the text, making it ineligible for deference after Kisor.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether defendants must meet all three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) to be disqualified from safety-valve relief, or whether meeting any single criterion suffices. This split directly affects mandatory minimum sentencing for drug offenses and creates geographic disparities in criminal sentencing.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three required to disqualify
positions.summary: Holds that 'and' means 'and,' so a defendant is disqualified from safety-valve relief only if all three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) are met.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that meeting any single criminal-history criterion listed in § 3553(f)(1) is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief, despite the statutory use of 'and.'

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state schedule covers substances not listed on the federal Controlled Substances Act schedules.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' is limited to substances controlled under federal law or encompasses any substance controlled under state law, even if not federally scheduled. This split affects career-offender and other sentencing enhancements for defendants with state drug convictions.

positions.label: State-law substances suffice
positions.summary: Holds that 'controlled substance offense' under § 4B1.2(b) includes offenses under state law without requiring the substance to be federally controlled, as there is no textual basis to graft a federal limitation onto the guideline.

positions.label: Must match federal schedules
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the substance is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

circuits.name: First Circuit
circuits.caseName: Referenced in Henderson circuit split discussion

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law (such as the First Step Act's changes to § 924(c) stacking) can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A), and whether the Sentencing Commission has authority to define it as such.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether changes in law that Congress chose not to make retroactive can serve as a basis for compassionate release, and whether the Sentencing Commission's 2024 policy statement (§ 1B1.13(b)(6)) authorizing courts to consider such changes exceeds the Commission's statutory authority. This affects thousands of federal prisoners serving lengthy sentences under now-repealed mandatory minimums.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot be extraordinary and compelling
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law cannot contribute to a finding of 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for compassionate release, and that the Sentencing Commission's policy statement attempting to authorize such consideration exceeds its statutory authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes can be considered
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law can be considered as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis, particularly in combination with other factors, and that the Sentencing Commission has authority to define such circumstances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners must use habeas corpus (28 U.S.C. § 2241) rather than civil rights actions to challenge conditions of confinement or BOP decisions that affect the duration or terms of imprisonment, such as earned time credit calculations under the First Step Act.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for prisoners challenging decisions that affect the fact or duration of confinement, or whether civil rights actions (Bivens or § 1983) may also be used. This split affects how federal prisoners can challenge BOP decisions regarding First Step Act time credits and transfer to prerelease custody.

positions.label: Habeas is exclusive for duration-of-confinement challenges
positions.summary: Holds that when a prisoner challenges a decision affecting the fact or duration of confinement, the sole federal remedy is habeas corpus, and civil rights actions are not available.

positions.label: Civil rights actions may also be available
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may use civil rights actions to challenge conditions or BOP decisions even when the relief might affect the duration of confinement, particularly when habeas would be inadequate.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Referenced in Spencer v. Haynes circuit split discussion

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the civil or criminal deadline for filing a notice of appeal applies to orders on Hyde Amendment motions for attorney's fees in criminal cases.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (triggering the longer civil appeal deadline) or part of the criminal case itself (triggering the shorter criminal deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the civil notice-of-appeal deadline (60 days when the government is a party) applies.

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that Hyde Amendment motions are part of the criminal proceeding, so the criminal notice-of-appeal deadline (14 days) governs.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Referenced as minority view in Onamuti

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's property belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor when a Chapter 13 case is converted in good faith to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the appreciation in property value that occurs between a Chapter 13 filing and conversion to Chapter 7 belongs to the estate or the debtor. This split directly affects whether debtors who convert in good faith lose the benefit of property appreciation that occurred during their Chapter 13 case.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that under the plain language of § 348(f)(1)(A) and the broad scope of § 541(a), post-petition appreciation inures to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion, not to the debtor.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that the Bankruptcy Code's structure and legislative history establish that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation belongs to debtors who convert in good faith from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Referenced in Castleman dissent as opposing view

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly impose punishment for the supervised release violation itself when revoking supervised release under 18 U.S.C. § 3583, or whether revocation sentences may only serve the purposes of deterrence, incapacitation, and rehabilitation.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether punishment is a permissible purpose of a revocation sentence upon supervised release. The Sixth Circuit allows courts to expressly punish defendants for violations, while other circuits hold that revocation sentences may not be punitive. This affects hundreds of supervised release revocations annually.

positions.label: Punishment is permissible
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release when imposing revocation sentences, based on the precedent of United States v. Lewis.

positions.label: Punishment is not permissible
positions.summary: Holds that revocation of supervised release may not serve a purely punitive purpose; rather, revocation sentences should focus on deterrence, incapacitation, and rehabilitation.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: Referenced in Esteras dissent as opposing view

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the timing requirements for actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability under ERISA. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers participating in multiemployer pension plans, as the timing of assumption selection directly controls how much withdrawing employers must pay.

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that plan actuaries may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing the use of updated information in calculating withdrawal liability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions must be determined by the end of the prior plan year (the statutory measurement date), providing employers with greater predictability about potential liability.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether federal courts can apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the period of court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects sentencing calculations at revocation hearings for thousands of individuals who abscond each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled when a supervisee absconds, so the clock stops running and the supervised release period is extended by the time spent in fugitive status.

positions.label: No tolling — term continues to run
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory basis for tolling supervised release during absconding, so the term continues to run regardless of the supervisee's compliance or presence.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing successive motions under 28 U.S.C. § 2255.
splits.description: A longstanding 6-to-3 circuit split exists on whether federal prisoners face a categorical bar under § 2244(b)(1) on re-raising previously presented claims in successive § 2255 motions, in addition to the separate requirements of § 2255(h). If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners are categorically barred from raising any claim they previously presented; if not, they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, imposing a categorical bar in addition to § 2255(h)'s requirements.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, so they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates have standing to challenge election rules before an election takes place. The resolution affects whether pre-election challenges to voting procedures can proceed or must wait until after the election, with significant implications for mail-in voting rules and election administration nationwide.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates have Article III standing to bring pre-election challenges to state election laws that affect how ballots are counted, based on competitive injury or vote-dilution theories.

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates do not have Article III standing to challenge election rules pre-election because the alleged injury is too speculative or generalized.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that denial of a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable because medical privacy is a value of 'high order' that would be effectively unreviewable after final judgment. Other circuits have not uniformly recognized this category of collateral orders, creating potential disagreement on the scope of the collateral order doctrine for privacy-related sealing orders.

positions.label: Immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that denial of a motion to seal medical records is a collateral order immediately appealable under § 1291 because medical privacy is a value of high order that cannot be vindicated by delayed review.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that sealing orders generally do not satisfy the collateral order doctrine's requirements because privacy concerns can be addressed through other mechanisms or on appeal after final judgment.

circuits.name: First Circuit
circuits.caseName: Referenced in Abdelhady as recognizing strong privacy interest but not necessarily endorsing collateral order review

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The circuits have diverged on the standards for fair treatment, discrimination liability, and damages in business operations including hospitality, retail, and other service industries. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve the Second Circuit's approach to these legal questions, indicating a circuit split of sufficient importance.

positions.label: Second Circuit approach
positions.summary: Applies the Second Circuit's particular legal framework for evaluating discrimination and unfair treatment claims against business operators.

positions.label: Differing approach
positions.summary: Other circuits apply different legal standards for evaluating discrimination claims against hospitality and business establishments.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state law categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violates the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated sex-based biological advantages, and whether as-applied equal protection challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether categorical bans on transgender athlete participation survive intermediate scrutiny when applied to individuals who have undergone medical transition. The case also raises the broader question of whether sex-based classifications affecting transgender individuals warrant heightened scrutiny.

positions.label: Categorical ban violates Equal Protection as applied
positions.summary: Holds that a categorical ban fails intermediate scrutiny as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated biological advantages, because the state has not shown the ban is substantially related to its interest in competitive fairness for this subclass.

positions.label: Categorical ban does not violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that biological sex-based classifications in athletics are substantially related to the important governmental interest in fair competition and the safety of female athletes, even as applied to transgender women.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
